claim: Protein NƐ-lysine acetylation (Kac) modifications play crucial roles in diverse physiological and pathological functions in cells.
source: Protein NƐ-lysine acetylation (Kac) modifications play crucial roles in diverse physiological and pathological functions in cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of Kac modifications, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In prokaryotic cells, there are only two types of lysine deacetylases (KDACs) that are Zn2+- or NAD+-dependent.
source: In prokaryotic cells, there are only two types of lysine deacetylases (KDACs) that are Zn2+- or NAD+-dependent.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section discussing currently known bacterial KDACs.

claim: The KDAC activity of AhCobQ is located in an unidentified domain from 195 to 245 aa.
source: Furthermore, its KDAC activity is located in an unidentified domain (from 195 to 245 aa).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from truncation studies shown in Figure 4.

claim: AhCobQ has no homology with current known KDACs.
source: Interestingly, AhCobQ has no homology with current known KDACs, and no homologous protein was found in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 5.

claim: No homologous protein to AhCobQ was found in eukaryotic cells.
source: Interestingly, AhCobQ has no homology with current known KDACs, and no homologous protein was found in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is supported by PSI-BLAST analysis results described in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: AhCobQ has specific protein substrates in common with other known KDACs.
source: A protein substrate analysis showed that AhCobQ has specific protein substrates in common with other known KDACs, indicating that these KDACs can dynamically co-regulate the states of Kac proteins.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative acetylome data shown in Figure 6.

claim: AhCobQ positively regulates isocitrate dehydrogenase (ICD) enzymatic activity at the K388 site.
source: Microbiological methods employed in this study affirmed AhCobQ's positive regulation of isocitrate dehydrogenase (ICD) enzymatic activity at the K388 site, implicating AhCobQ in the modulation of bacterial enzymatic activities.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: The deletion of ahcobB did not affect the hemolytic ability of A. hydrophila.
source: When compared to the wild-type strain (WT), the deletion of ahcobB did not affect the hemolytic or swarming ability of A. hydrophila.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The deletion of ahcobB did not affect the swarming ability of A. hydrophila.
source: When compared to the wild-type strain (WT), the deletion of ahcobB did not affect the hemolytic or swarming ability of A. hydrophila.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ΔahcobQ did not affect the hemolytic ability of A. hydrophila.
source: Notably, ΔahcobQ did not affect the hemolytic ability either but significantly increased the swarming ability (Figure 1B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ΔahcobQ significantly increased the swarming ability of A. hydrophila.
source: Notably, ΔahcobQ did not affect the hemolytic ability either but significantly increased the swarming ability (Figure 1B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ΔahcobB sharply increased bacterial biofilm formation ability.
source: Most interestingly, ΔahcobB sharply increased, while ΔahcobQ significantly decreased, the bacterial biofilm formation ability (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ΔahcobQ significantly decreased bacterial biofilm formation ability.
source: Most interestingly, ΔahcobB sharply increased, while ΔahcobQ significantly decreased, the bacterial biofilm formation ability (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CobB and CobQ in A. hydrophila may play different roles in biological functions.
source: These results indicated that CobB and CobQ in A. hydrophila may play different roles in biological functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential phenotypic effects observed in deletion mutants shown in Figure 1.

claim: AhCobB belongs to a NAD+-dependent protein deacylase sirtuin family.
source: AhCobB (UniProt ID A0KKN9) belongs to a well-known NAD+-dependent protein deacylase sirtuin family and shares a highly homologous SIR2 domain with CobB sirtuins in many bacterial species, such as E. coli (NPD_ECOLI), S. typhimurium (NPD_SALTY), Pseudomonas nitroreducens (A0A246F352_9PSED), and even seven types of sirtuins in humans (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by homology analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AhCobB shares a highly homologous SIR2 domain with CobB sirtuins in many bacterial species and human sirtuins.
source: AhCobB (UniProt ID A0KKN9) belongs to a well-known NAD+-dependent protein deacylase sirtuin family and shares a highly homologous SIR2 domain with CobB sirtuins in many bacterial species, such as E. coli (NPD_ECOLI), S. typhimurium (NPD_SALTY), Pseudomonas nitroreducens (A0A246F352_9PSED), and even seven types of sirtuins in humans (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by homology analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AhCobQ shares an AAA_31 ATPase domain with several homologous proteins.
source: However, AhCobQ (UniProt ID A0KI27) shares an AAA_31 ATPase domain with several homologous proteins, such as cobalamin biosynthesis protein CobQ in P. nitroreducens (A0A246FC44_9PSED), probable plasmid partitioning protein in P. aeruginosa (G3XCW7_PSEAE), and chromosome partitioning ATPase in S. typhimurium (A0A0F6B556_SALT1).
evidence: This is supported by domain analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AhCobQ shares homology with Soj protein and cell division inhibitor MinD in A. hydrophila.
source: Moreover, AhCobQ also shares homology with Soj protein (A0KQY7_AERHH) and cell division inhibitor MinD (A0KK56_AERHH) in A. hydrophila as well (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by homology analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The deletion of ahcobQ significantly increased the whole protein lysine acetylation levels in A. hydrophila cells.
source: Dot blot and western blot experiments showed that the deletion of ahcobQ or ahcobB both significantly increased the whole protein lysine acetylation levels in A. hydrophila cells (Figure 2C and D)
evidence: This is supported by dot blot and western blot data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The deletion of ahcobB significantly increased the whole protein lysine acetylation levels in A. hydrophila cells.
source: Dot blot and western blot experiments showed that the deletion of ahcobQ or ahcobB both significantly increased the whole protein lysine acetylation levels in A. hydrophila cells (Figure 2C and D)
evidence: This is supported by dot blot and western blot data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: AhCobB significantly deacetylated Kac-BSA in the presence of NAD+.
source: As a positive control, AhCobB and AhAcuC significantly deacetylated Kac-BSA in the presence of NAD+ or Zn2 + buffer, which met our expectations.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: AhAcuC significantly deacetylated Kac-BSA in the presence of Zn2+.
source: As a positive control, AhCobB and AhAcuC significantly deacetylated Kac-BSA in the presence of NAD+ or Zn2 + buffer, which met our expectations.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: AhCobQ clearly deacetylated Kac-BSA regardless of whether NAD+ or Zn2+ were present.
source: However, AhCobQ clearly deacetylated Kac-BSA regardless of whether NAD+ or Zn2+ were present (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: The KDAC activity of AhCobB was inhibited when the sirtuin inhibitor nicotinamide (NAM) was added.
source: Moreover, the KDAC activity of AhCobB was inhibited when the sirtuin inhibitor nicotinamide (NAM) was added, but this did not affect the deacetylase activity of AhCobQ (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: NAM did not affect the deacetylase activity of AhCobQ.
source: Moreover, the KDAC activity of AhCobB was inhibited when the sirtuin inhibitor nicotinamide (NAM) was added, but this did not affect the deacetylase activity of AhCobQ (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The introduction of the metal ion chelator EDTA had no discernible effect on the deacetylase activity of AhCobQ.
source: Furthermore, the introduction of the metal ion chelator, EDTA, had no discernible effect on the deacetylase activity of AhCobQ (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The KDAC activity of AhCobQ was ATP-independent.
source: The results demonstrated that the KDAC activity of AhCobQ was ATP-independent, suggesting its enzymatic activity was downstream of the ATPase domain.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The MS intensities of at least 15 Kac peptides in BSA were significantly decreased after AhCobQ treatment.
source: The results showed that the MS intensities of at least 15 Kac peptides in BSA were significantly decreased after AhCobQ treatment.
evidence: This is supported by LC MS/MS data referenced in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: AhCobQ is not a hydrolase that hydrolyzes target proteins but likely a protein deacetylase similar to AhCobB.
source: These results indicate that AhCobQ is not a hydrolase that hydrolyzes target proteins but likely a protein deacetylase similar to AhCobB.
evidence: This is inferred from LC MS/MS data shown in Figure 3 demonstrating that AhCobQ removes acetyl groups without hydrolyzing peptides.

claim: The 179–264 aa protein fragment of AhCobQ showed NAD+- and Zn2+-independent deacetylase activity.
source: To our surprise, the 179–264 aa protein fragment but not the 1–179 aa fragment showed NAD+- and Zn2+-independent deacetylase activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 1–179 aa protein fragment of AhCobQ did not show deacetylase activity.
source: To our surprise, the 179–264 aa protein fragment but not the 1–179 aa fragment showed NAD+- and Zn2+-independent deacetylase activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The deacetylase activity of AhCobQ may be in the 195–245 aa range.
source: As shown in Figure 4, the 1–179 aa, 200–255 aa, and 189–240 aa shortened proteins disrupted the deacetylase activity of AhCobQ to some extent, whereas the 179–264 aa, 189–264 aa, 199–264 aa, 195–264 aa, 195–255 aa, 189–245 aa, 189–250 aa, 189–255 aa, and 189–264 aa shortened proteins did not, indicating that the deacetylase activity may be in the 195–245 aa range.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from truncation studies shown in Figure 4.

claim: The KDAC activity domain (195–245 aa) of AhCobQ does not share homology with Soj protein, site-determining protein, and ParA family protein in A. hydrophila.
source: Interestingly, although the full amino acid sequence of AhCobQ (1–254 aa) is homologous with Soj protein (A0KQYT), site-determining protein (A0KI19 and A0KK56), and ParA family protein (A0KQG8) in A. hydrophila, the KDAC activity domain (195–245 aa) does not share homology with these proteins, which suggests the different biological roles among them.
evidence: This is inferred from bioinformatics analysis comparing the KDAC domain with homologous proteins.

claim: AhCobQ (195–245 aa) shares homology with several prokaryotic species, most of which are marine prokaryotes.
source: Moreover, AhCobQ (195–245 aa) also shares homology with several prokaryotic species, such as Aeromonas sp., Aliivibrio sp., Enterovibri sp., Oceanimonas sp., Photobacterium sp., and Vibrio sp., most of which are marine prokaryotes based on a PSI-BLAST program searching, but the search failed to find homologous proteins in eukaryotic cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by PSI-BLAST analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The deletion of ahcobQ led to increased abundances at 52 Kac sites corresponding to 47 Kac proteins.
source: When compared to WT, the deletion of ahcobQ, ahcobB, and ahacuC led to increased abundances at 52 Kac sites (corresponding to 47 Kac proteins), 370 Kac sites (291 proteins), and 197 Kac sites (176 proteins), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative acetylome data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The deletion of ahcobB led to increased abundances at 370 Kac sites corresponding to 291 proteins.
source: When compared to WT, the deletion of ahcobQ, ahcobB, and ahacuC led to increased abundances at 52 Kac sites (corresponding to 47 Kac proteins), 370 Kac sites (291 proteins), and 197 Kac sites (176 proteins), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative acetylome data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The deletion of ahacuC led to increased abundances at 197 Kac sites corresponding to 176 proteins.
source: When compared to WT, the deletion of ahcobQ, ahcobB, and ahacuC led to increased abundances at 52 Kac sites (corresponding to 47 Kac proteins), 370 Kac sites (291 proteins), and 197 Kac sites (176 proteins), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative acetylome data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There were 19 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahacuC strains.
source: Moreover, there were 19 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahacuC strains, 10 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahcobB strains, 69 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobB and ΔahacuC strains, and four peptides common among the ΔahcobQ, ΔahcobB, and ΔahacuC strains (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There were 10 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahcobB strains.
source: Moreover, there were 19 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahacuC strains, 10 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahcobB strains, 69 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobB and ΔahacuC strains, and four peptides common among the ΔahcobQ, ΔahcobB, and ΔahacuC strains (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There were 69 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobB and ΔahacuC strains.
source: Moreover, there were 19 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahacuC strains, 10 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahcobB strains, 69 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobB and ΔahacuC strains, and four peptides common among the ΔahcobQ, ΔahcobB, and ΔahacuC strains (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There were four peptides common among the ΔahcobQ, ΔahcobB, and ΔahacuC strains.
source: Moreover, there were 19 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahacuC strains, 10 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobQ and ΔahcobB strains, 69 increased Kac peptides common between the ΔahcobB and ΔahacuC strains, and four peptides common among the ΔahcobQ, ΔahcobB, and ΔahacuC strains (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only 531 Kac peptides are directly regulated by the three deacetylases, accounting for 10.28% of all 3163 Kac peptides identified.
source: We also found that there were only 531 Kac peptides directly regulated by these three deacetylases, which is only a small proportion of the total Kac peptides (accounting for 10.28% of all 3163 Kac peptides identified in the current study), indicating the presence of other unknown KDACs in this bacterium.
evidence: This is inferred from quantitative acetylome data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There are other unknown KDACs in A. hydrophila.
source: We also found that there were only 531 Kac peptides directly regulated by these three deacetylases, which is only a small proportion of the total Kac peptides (accounting for 10.28% of all 3163 Kac peptides identified in the current study), indicating the presence of other unknown KDACs in this bacterium.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only a small proportion of Kac peptides are regulated by the three known KDACs.

claim: Biosynthesis of amino acids and antibiotics was enriched in the unique upregulated Kac proteins in the ΔahcobQ strain.
source: A KEGG pathway analysis showed that biosynthesis of amino acids and antibiotics was enriched in the unique upregulated Kac proteins in the ΔahcobQ strain (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AhCobQ can significantly deacetylate ICD at K388.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, AhCobQ can significantly deacetylated ICD at K388, while the other two deacetylases, AhCobB and AhAcuC didn't.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: AhCobB did not deacetylate ICD at K388.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, AhCobQ can significantly deacetylated ICD at K388, while the other two deacetylases, AhCobB and AhAcuC didn't.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: AhAcuC did not deacetylate ICD at K388.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, AhCobQ can significantly deacetylated ICD at K388, while the other two deacetylases, AhCobB and AhAcuC didn't.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Kac at K388 of ICD significantly decreased the product of NADPH with the addition of NADP+ substrate.
source: When compared with unKac ICD protein, the Kac at K388 of ICD significantly decreased the product of NADPH with the addition of NADP+ substrate, which indicates the Kac at K388 negatively regulates the enzymatic activity of ICD.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Kac at K388 negatively regulates the enzymatic activity of ICD.
source: When compared with unKac ICD protein, the Kac at K388 of ICD significantly decreased the product of NADPH with the addition of NADP+ substrate, which indicates the Kac at K388 negatively regulates the enzymatic activity of ICD.
evidence: This is inferred from enzymatic activity assay data showing decreased NADPH production in acetylated ICD.

claim: The addition of AhCobQ significantly increased the enzymatic activity of K388 acetylated ICD.
source: Moreover, the adding of AhCobQ significantly increased the enzymatic activity of K388 acetylated ICD and quickly reached the platform period in 10 min, while AhCobB and AhAcuC didn't affect ICD enzymatic activity (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: AhCobB did not affect ICD enzymatic activity.
source: Moreover, the adding of AhCobQ significantly increased the enzymatic activity of K388 acetylated ICD and quickly reached the platform period in 10 min, while AhCobB and AhAcuC didn't affect ICD enzymatic activity (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: AhAcuC did not affect ICD enzymatic activity.
source: Moreover, the adding of AhCobQ significantly increased the enzymatic activity of K388 acetylated ICD and quickly reached the platform period in 10 min, while AhCobB and AhAcuC didn't affect ICD enzymatic activity (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: There are currently at least 18 types of HDACs in four classes (I–IV) in mammals.
source: There are currently at least 18 types of HDACs in four classes (I–IV) in mammals and four plant-specific histone deacetylase 2 (HD2) members in the plant (Yoshida et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2017 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: There are four plant-specific histone deacetylase 2 (HD2) members in plants.
source: There are currently at least 18 types of HDACs in four classes (I–IV) in mammals and four plant-specific histone deacetylase 2 (HD2) members in the plant (Yoshida et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2017 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: HDAC types I, II, and IV are Zn2+-dependent.
source: Of these, HDAC types I, II, and IV are Zn2+-dependent, while type III deacetylases are NAD+-dependent sirtuins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDAC classification.

claim: Type III deacetylases are NAD+-dependent sirtuins.
source: Of these, HDAC types I, II, and IV are Zn2+-dependent, while type III deacetylases are NAD+-dependent sirtuins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDAC classification.

claim: Sirtuins can be divided into seven types (SIRT 1–7) distributed in different compartments of eukaryotic cells.
source: Moreover, sirtuins can be divided into seven types (SIRT 1–7), which are distributed in different compartments of eukaryotic cells and perform important biological functions (Narita et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Narita et al., 2019.

claim: ABHD14B is a novel KDAC that deacetylates non-histone substrates and influences glucose metabolism in mammals.
source: Besides these, ABHD14B, a novel KDAC, was reported to deacetylate non-histone substrates and influence glucose metabolism in mammals (Rajendran et al., 2022; Rajendran et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rajendran et al., 2022 and Rajendran et al., 2020.

claim: The currently known KDACs in bacteria include Zn2+-dependent RpLdaA or Kdac1, Zn2+-dependent AcuC, and NAD+-dependent sirtuin family proteins.
source: The currently known KDACs in bacteria include Zn2 +-dependent RpLdaA or Kdac1 (homologous to eukaryotic type II KDACs), Zn2+-dependent AcuC (homologous to type I), and NAD+-dependent sirtuin (homologous to type III) family proteins (Watson and Christianson, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watson and Christianson, 2023.

claim: Sirtuins are the most widely distributed KDACs in many bacterial species.
source: Sirtuins, represented by Escherichia coli CobB, are the most widely distributed KDACs in many bacterial species and are involved in the regulation of a variety of important physiological functions (Burckhardt et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burckhardt et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020b.

claim: Since the first report of the deacetylase function of CobB in Salmonella typhimurium in 1998, only two types (three classes) of KDACs have been confirmed in bacteria.
source: However, since the first report of the deacetylase function of CobB in Salmonella typhimurium in 1998, only two types (three classes) of KDACs have been confirmed in bacteria (Tsang and Escalante-Semerena, 1998; Macek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsang and Escalante-Semerena, 1998 and Macek et al., 2019.

claim: AhCobQ is annotated as a CobQ/CobB/MinD/ParA family protein in the UniProt database.
source: Interestingly, although this protein is described as a CobQ/CobB/MinD/ParA family protein in the UniProt database, it is homologous with cobyric acid synthase in other bacterial species but shares no homology with CobB sirtuin family proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about database annotation.

claim: AhCobQ is homologous with cobyric acid synthase in other bacterial species.
source: Interestingly, although this protein is described as a CobQ/CobB/MinD/ParA family protein in the UniProt database, it is homologous with cobyric acid synthase in other bacterial species but shares no homology with CobB sirtuin family proteins.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis.

claim: AhCobQ shares no homology with CobB sirtuin family proteins.
source: Interestingly, although this protein is described as a CobQ/CobB/MinD/ParA family protein in the UniProt database, it is homologous with cobyric acid synthase in other bacterial species but shares no homology with CobB sirtuin family proteins.
evidence: This is supported by homology analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: AhCobQ deacetylated lysine-acetylated sites common to AhCobB sirtuin and AhAcuC in A. hydrophila.
source: In addition to deacetylating lysine-acetylated sites common to AhCobB (UniProt ID A0KKN9, gene ID AHA_2317) sirtuin and another deacetylase AhAcuC (UniProt ID A0KLZ2, gene ID AHA_2788) in A. hydrophila, we also confirmed that AhCobQ deacetylated specific lysine-acetylated sites as did other KDACs, even in the same protein.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative acetylome data shown in Figure 6 and validation experiments in Figure 7.

claim: AhCobQ deacetylated specific lysine-acetylated sites different from other KDACs, even in the same protein.
source: In addition to deacetylating lysine-acetylated sites common to AhCobB (UniProt ID A0KKN9, gene ID AHA_2317) sirtuin and another deacetylase AhAcuC (UniProt ID A0KLZ2, gene ID AHA_2788) in A. hydrophila, we also confirmed that AhCobQ deacetylated specific lysine-acetylated sites as did other KDACs, even in the same protein.
evidence: This is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: There are two distinct CobB annotations in the UniProt database: NAD-dependent protein deacylase and ATP-dependent a,c-diamide synthase.
source: Actually, CobB has a conflicting naming phenomenon in the UniProt annotation. There are two distinct CobB annotations in the UniProt database: one is the well-known NAD-dependent protein deacylase, such as NPD_ECOLI in E. coli, and the other is the ATP-dependent a,c-diamide synthase, such as CobB_SINSX in Sinorhizobium sp. that plays an important role in cobalamin biosynthesis (Galperin and Grishin, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galperin and Grishin, 2000 and database analysis.

claim: In some bacterial species, a,c-diamide synthase is also annotated as CbiA.
source: In some bacterial species, a,c-diamide synthase is also annotated as CbiA (such as CBIA_SALTY, for example), indicating the controversial assignment of CobB.
evidence: This is a statement about database annotation variability.

claim: There is not an a,c-diamide synthase homologous protein in A. hydrophila ATCC 7966.
source: Interestingly, there is not an a,c-diamide synthase homologous protein in A. hydrophila ATCC 7966, and the CobB annotation in A. hydrophila ATCC 7966 is specific for NAD-dependent protein deacylase.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis of the A. hydrophila genome.

claim: The CobB annotation in A. hydrophila ATCC 7966 is specific for NAD-dependent protein deacylase.
source: Interestingly, there is not an a,c-diamide synthase homologous protein in A. hydrophila ATCC 7966, and the CobB annotation in A. hydrophila ATCC 7966 is specific for NAD-dependent protein deacylase.
evidence: This is based on database annotation and functional characterization.

claim: The CobQ protein is annotated as cobyric acid synthase and belongs to a,c-diamide synthase (CobB or CbiA) but not the sirtuin protein (CobB) family.
source: In general, the CobQ protein is annotated as cobyric acid synthase and belongs to a,c-diamide synthase (CobB or CbiA) but not the sirtuin protein (CobB) family.
evidence: This is based on database annotation and homology analysis.

claim: The role of AhCobQ is unknown because A. hydrophila may import rather than synthesize cobalamin (vitamin B12).
source: The role of AhCobQ is unknown to date because A. hydrophila may import rather than synthesize cobalamin (vitamin B12) (Seshadri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seshadri et al., 2006.

claim: 9.9% of the acetylated proteins (312/3164 Kac protein) were regulated by ahcobB.
source: The results showed that 9.9% of the acetylated proteins (312/3164 Kac protein) were regulated by ahcobB, which is consistent with the proportion in the E. coli cobB mutant and the previous conclusion that CobB is the predominate deacetylase in some bacterial species (Weinert et al., 2013; AbouElfetouh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative acetylome data and citations to Weinert et al., 2013 and AbouElfetouh et al., 2015.

claim: CobB is the predominate deacetylase in some bacterial species.
source: The results showed that 9.9% of the acetylated proteins (312/3164 Kac protein) were regulated by ahcobB, which is consistent with the proportion in the E. coli cobB mutant and the previous conclusion that CobB is the predominate deacetylase in some bacterial species (Weinert et al., 2013; AbouElfetouh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weinert et al., 2013 and AbouElfetouh et al., 2015.

claim: AhCobQ and AhCobB co-regulated the same Kac sites on ArcA-2 (Arginine deiminase).
source: Moreover, AhCobQ and AhCobB also co-regulated the same Kac sites on ArcA-2 (Arginine deiminase), indicating that the cooperation of these KDACs may play an important role during the maintenance of cellular acetylation homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The cooperation of KDACs may play an important role during the maintenance of cellular acetylation homeostasis.
source: Moreover, AhCobQ and AhCobB also co-regulated the same Kac sites on ArcA-2 (Arginine deiminase), indicating that the cooperation of these KDACs may play an important role during the maintenance of cellular acetylation homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple KDACs can regulate the same acetylation sites.

claim: GyrB K331 is located in the ATPase domain that is responsible for supercoiling DNA.
source: The 3D structure prediction showed that GyrB K331 is located in the ATPase domain that is responsible for supercoiling DNA, whereas K449 is located in the Toprim domain that is required for the interaction with GyrA (Brino et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by 3D structure prediction and citation to Brino et al., 2000.

claim: GyrB K449 is located in the Toprim domain that is required for the interaction with GyrA.
source: The 3D structure prediction showed that GyrB K331 is located in the ATPase domain that is responsible for supercoiling DNA, whereas K449 is located in the Toprim domain that is required for the interaction with GyrA (Brino et al., 2000).
